Order book / DOM.long:
The order book, shown on trading platforms as the DOM — depth of market — is the live list of resting limit orders at each price: bids stacked below the current price, offers stacked above, with the size waiting at every level.

What it shows is genuine: actual committed orders, updated in real time. What people infer from it is where the trouble starts. Displayed size is not intention — large orders can be pulled the instant price approaches, and orders can be layered to create an appearance of interest that vanishes on contact. Iceberg orders invert the problem: the real size is deliberately hidden, showing only a sliver. So the book reliably shows where orders are resting right now, and unreliably shows what will actually trade there.

For most retail purposes the book's honest uses are practical: reading the spread, judging whether your own size would move the market, and seeing liquidity thin out ahead of news.

Where people get fooled: trading the display as a forecast. A wall of bids looks like support until it is pulled — and pulling it may have been the point. The tape of executed trades tells you what happened; the book tells you what someone currently claims they might do.
Order book / DOM.usage: Generally read for spread, depth and your own likely impact; displayed size is a claim, not a commitment.

Last traded price.long:
The last traded price is the price of the most recent completed transaction — the number the chart plots, the ticker displays, and most people mean when they say the price.

It is worth being precise about what it is not. It is not the price you can trade at: buying happens at the ask and selling at the bid, and the last trade sits at or between them. In a liquid market the distinction costs a tick; in a thin one it can be substantial, and the gap is largest exactly when acting feels most urgent. The last price is also backward-looking by definition — in a fast market it lags the quotes, and in an illiquid instrument it can be minutes or hours stale, describing a transaction from a different regime entirely.

Mark-to-market valuations, platform P&L displays and alert triggers all typically run off the last price, which is why an account's displayed value can differ from what liquidating it would actually raise.

Where people get fooled: treating the last price as executable. The chart says one number; the fill says another, and the difference — spread plus slippage — is a cost every strategy pays and most backtests forget to charge.
Last traded price.usage: Generally the number charts plot and P&L marks against; executable prices are the bid and ask either side of it.

Mid price.long:
The mid price is the midpoint between the best bid and best ask. If the bid is 100.00 and the ask 100.10, the mid is 100.05 — a price at which nobody is actually offering to trade.

Its uses are real despite that. The mid is the least biased single estimate of where the market currently values the instrument, which is why institutional execution quality is measured against it: a buy filled below mid beat the market's resting state, one filled at the ask paid the full crossing cost. Options and illiquid instruments quote such wide spreads that the mid is the only sensible reference for value, and limit orders are often worked at or near it to split the spread with the counterparty.

The mid also makes the cost of impatience explicit: crossing the spread costs half the spread relative to mid, on every entry and every exit, and that toll compounds with trade frequency.

Where people get fooled: valuing a position at mid and expecting to exit there. The mid is an average of two prices you cannot trade at simultaneously; realising it requires someone to cross the spread toward you, which in a thin market may simply never happen at anything near the displayed midpoint.
Mid price.usage: Generally the reference for fair value and execution quality; trading at it requires patience or luck, since no one is quoted there.

Quote vs trade.long:
A quote is an offer to trade — a resting bid or ask with a size attached. A trade is a completed transaction. The distinction sounds pedantic and explains a surprising amount of market behaviour.

Quotes are free to make and free to cancel, so they carry limited commitment: the visible book is a set of revocable claims, and most quotes are cancelled rather than filled — in modern electronic markets, overwhelmingly so. Trades are the record of what actually happened: someone paid the crossing cost, size changed hands, and the print is permanent. Price discovery lives in the interaction — quotes propose, trades dispose — and the two data feeds are literally separate in market-data plumbing, with quote traffic dwarfing trade traffic.

Reading the two together is what tape reading means: heavy quoting with no trades is a market posturing; steady prints into a large resting quote is a market testing whether the claim is real.

Where people get fooled: charting tools blur the line. A chart built from trades shows what transacted; indicators built on quote data show what was claimed. And a level defended by quotes that vanish on approach was never defended at all — the commitment existed only until it was tested.
Quote vs trade.usage: Generally: quotes are revocable claims, trades are settled fact; tape reading is watching how the two interact.

Long-only vs long-short.long:
A long-only approach can profit only from prices rising: buy, hold, sell higher. A long-short approach can also sell short — borrowing or synthetically selling what it does not own — to profit from falls.

The structural differences run deeper than direction count. Long-only has an asymmetric loss floor: a position can lose at most its value. Short positions have no such ceiling — the price of what you owe can rise without limit, which is why shorts are managed more tightly and why forced covering produces squeezes. Long-only also collects the equity market's structural upward drift over long horizons, while shorting fights that drift and pays borrow fees or funding for the privilege. Long-short's genuine advantage is the ability to express relative views — long the strong instrument, short the weak one — which removes broad market direction from the bet entirely.

Most retail products blur the line: CFDs, futures and perps make shorting one click, without the borrow mechanics shares require.

Where people get fooled: symmetry assumptions. Shorting is not buying upside-down — the loss profile inverts, time works against you in drifting markets, and the crowd exiting a losing short pushes the price further against the remaining shorts. The click is symmetric; the risk is not.
Long-only vs long-short.usage: Generally a structural choice: long-only rides drift with capped loss, long-short adds relative bets at the cost of uncapped short risk.

Instrument selection.long:
Instrument selection is the choice of what to trade — which market, which product, which specific contract — made before any question of when or how. It quietly sets most of the cost and risk structure the strategy then lives inside.

The selection criteria that matter are unglamorous. Liquidity: the spread and depth decide the toll paid on every single trade, and a strategy that works on a tight-spread index future can be identical logic and unprofitable on a wide-spread altcoin. Costs beyond spread: commissions, swaps, funding, borrow. Volatility relative to account size: an instrument whose ordinary daily range exceeds what the account can absorb forces either oversized risk or sub-minimum positions. Session fit: a Perth trader picking an instrument whose liquid hours land at 3am has selected a lifestyle problem. And product structure: expiry, rollover, funding resets — each adds mechanics the strategy must handle.

One honest simplification: most strategies are not instrument-specific, but their cost arithmetic is, so the same idea lives or dies by this choice.

Where people get fooled: selecting by excitement. The instrument that moves most attracts attention precisely because it moves — but range without depth is cost in disguise, and the exciting chart charges admission on every entry, exit and overnight hold.
Instrument selection.usage: Generally decided on liquidity, total cost, volatility-to-account fit and session timing — before strategy logic enters the discussion.

Swing high / swing low.long:
A swing high is a bar whose high stands above the bars either side of it; a swing low, the mirror. They are the pivots from which structure is drawn: trends defined by their sequence, support and resistance anchored at them, stops tucked behind them.

The definition's honesty depends on one parameter: how many bars either side must be lower or higher for the pivot to count. A one-bar swing marks dozens of pivots per session; a ten-bar swing marks a handful per week — same chart, different structure. Every rule built on swings inherits that choice, and two traders disagreeing about the trend are usually just running different pivot widths without knowing it. Fixing the parameter and applying it mechanically is what makes swing-based rules testable at all.

Swings are also where stop orders congregate, precisely because the logic of placing them behind structure is taught everywhere — which is why moves through obvious swings so often accelerate briefly and reverse: triggered stops, then vacuum.

Where people get fooled: the pivot only exists once the bars after it have closed. In real time, the swing forms with a delay of however many confirming bars the definition demands — so structure drawn live keeps moving, and structure drawn in hindsight looks far cleaner than anything that was tradeable at the time.
Swing high / swing low.usage: Generally the pivots structure is drawn from; the confirming-bar count is a parameter that changes everything built on top.
